summary: Ibutilide fumarate is an intravenous class III antiarrhythmic indicated for the rapid conversion of recent-onset atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter to sinus rhythm. Patients 60 kg or more receive 1 mg (one vial) infused over 10 minutes; those under 60 kg receive 0.01 mg/kg (0.1 mL/kg). The infusion is stopped as soon as the arrhythmia terminates or if sustained/nonsustained VT or marked QT/QTc prolongation occurs; a second 10-minute infusion of equal strength may be given 10 minutes after the first if the arrhythmia persists. Ibutilide can cause potentially fatal arrhythmias, particularly sustained polymorphic ventricular tachycardia/torsades de pointes in association with QT prolongation (about 1.7% in trials). It must be given only with continuous ECG monitoring by personnel trained to manage acute ventricular arrhythmias, with patients monitored for at least 4 hours after infusion or until QTc returns to baseline. Atrial fibrillation of more than 2-3 days' duration requires adequate anticoagulation, generally for at least 2 weeks.
indications: Rapid conversion of atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter of recent onset to sinus rhythm

dosage.n: Stop as soon as arrhythmia terminates or if VT/marked QT prolongation occurs

dosage.r: Arrhythmia not terminated 10 min after first infusion
dosage.d: A second infusion of equal strength (1 mg or 0.01 mg/kg)
dosage.t: Over 10 minutes, 10 minutes after completing the first infusion
dosage.n: Do not give if QT markedly prolonged or VT occurs

admin: Correct hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia before administration
Administer undiluted or diluted in 50 mL of diluent; infuse over 10 minutes
Stop the infusion immediately when the arrhythmia terminates or if sustained/nonsustained VT or marked QT/QTc prolongation develops
Provide continuous ECG monitoring during and for at least 4 hours after the infusion, or until QTc returns to baseline; longer if any arrhythmia is noted
Have a defibrillator and drugs to treat torsades (IV magnesium) immediately available
Ensure AF of >2-3 days' duration is adequately anticoagulated (generally >=2 weeks) before conversion
moa: Ibutilide is a class III antiarrhythmic that prolongs the duration of the cardiac action potential and increases atrial and ventricular refractoriness. Unlike pure potassium-channel blockers, its main electrophysiologic action is activation of a slow, predominantly sodium, inward current during the plateau of the action potential, with a contribution from delay of the rapid delayed-rectifier potassium current (IKr). The net effect is delayed repolarisation, prolongation of the QT interval, and termination of re-entrant atrial arrhythmias. This same prolongation of repolarisation underlies its proarrhythmic potential for torsades de pointes.

absolute: Polymorphic VT / history of torsades de pointes with QT prolongation
relative: Concomitant QT-prolonging drugs (class Ia and other class III antiarrhythmics)
Significant structural heart disease, marked bradycardia, sick sinus syndrome
monitor: Heart rate and rhythm for VT/torsades

preg: Human data are limited. Animal studies showed adverse developmental effects (teratogenicity and embryofetal toxicity) at high maternal doses. Use in pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: It is not known whether ibutilide is excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions, caution is advised and a decision should be made whether to nurse or withhold the single dose.
renal: Ibutilide is rapidly metabolised; renal elimination of unchanged drug is minor, so no specific dosage adjustment is required in renal impairment. Standard ECG/electrolyte precautions still apply.
hepatic: Ibutilide is extensively metabolised by the liver. No specific dosage recommendation is provided, but caution is advised in significant hepatic impairment because of altered clearance and proarrhythmic risk.

major: Class Ia antiarrhythmics (disopyramide, quinidine, procainamide) - do not give concomitantly or within 4 h post-infusion; additive prolongation of refractoriness
Other class III antiarrhythmics (amiodarone, sotalol) - additive QT prolongation; avoid concomitant use
Other QT-prolonging drugs (certain phenothiazines, tricyclic/tetracyclic antidepressants, some antihistamines, macrolides, fluoroquinolones) - increased torsades risk
moderate: Digoxin - supraventricular arrhythmias from digoxin toxicity may mask cardiotoxicity; interpret ECG carefully
minor: Drugs causing hypokalaemia (diuretics) - increase proarrhythmic risk indirectly
interactions.alcohol: Not relevant to single supervised IV administration

serious: Sustained polymorphic ventricular tachycardia / torsades de pointes (can be fatal)
AV block, bundle-branch block, marked bradycardia
emergency: Torsades de pointes / sustained polymorphic VT requiring cardioversion
Symptomatic bradyarrhythmia or high-grade AV block

monitoring: Continuous ECG with QT/QTc throughout infusion and for at least 4 hours afterward (longer if any ectopy/arrhythmia)
Serum potassium and magnesium - correct before dosing
Heart rate, rhythm and blood pressure
Conversion to sinus rhythm (to stop the infusion)
counsel: This is a one-time injection given in hospital to try to restore a normal heart rhythm
You will be watched on a heart monitor during and for several hours after the injection
Tell the team at once if you feel faint, dizzy, have palpitations or chest discomfort
Some people need blood thinners before the procedure if the abnormal rhythm has lasted more than a couple of days
pk: Conversion usually occurs during the infusion or within about 30-90 minutes
Effect on the QT interval and conversion seen during/shortly after the 10-minute infusion
Single supervised dose; electrophysiologic effects (QT) resolve over hours
Store at controlled room temperature; protect per labeling
pearls: High torsades risk - give ONLY with continuous ECG monitoring and a defibrillator/IV magnesium available, by personnel trained in acute arrhythmia management
Correct hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia before dosing
Monitor for at least 4 hours after the infusion or until QTc returns to baseline
Most effective for AF/flutter of recent onset; arrhythmias >90 days are unlikely to convert
Anticoagulate AF of >2-3 days' duration (generally >=2 weeks) before cardioversion
missed: Not applicable - ibutilide is a single supervised intravenous dose, not a regularly scheduled self-administered medicine.
overdose: Overdose increases the risk of QT prolongation and torsades de pointes/ventricular arrhythmia. There is no specific antidote. Manage with continuous ECG monitoring, correction of electrolytes (IV magnesium for torsades), DC cardioversion/defibrillation for sustained VT, and supportive care.
